quote: are the same thing over twelve orders of magnitude apart
problem: The caption's main claim depends on 'orders of magnitude', a phrase the book has not used before (powers of ten), and it sits in a sentence that does not parse ('the same thing over ... apart'), so the reader has to re-read it to find the claim.
fix: 'are the same thing, though one trip is a million million times longer'
reason: The caption sentence reads badly. 'Are the same thing over twelve orders of magnitude apart' does not parse, and the claim is hidden in it. 'Orders of magnitude' is a common phrase (part-3 already uses it in the DOM chapter), so a gloss is not the main problem. The sentence structure is. Distances check out: 1 µm to 5,600 km is about 5.6e12, so 'over a million million times' is true.
judge_fix: A bit crossing a micrometre of chip wiring and a bit crossing 5,600 km of ocean are the same thing, a signal guided along a line in copper or in glass, though the second trip is over a million million times longer. (Keep the second caption sentence as is. The desc's 'more than twelve orders of magnitude apart' can stay, since it is not visible text.)

quote: That is the trick behind the twist.
problem: No earlier sentence says the two copper wires are twisted around each other, so 'the twist' points at nothing. The reader has to work it out backwards from 'The twist keeps neither wire systematically closer' two sentences later. The figure's drawn words never say 'twisted pair' either (only its <desc> does, and the figure comes after).
fix: say it first: the two wires are twisted around each other (a twisted pair)
reason: Verified in the packet. Nothing in ch8-substrates-p2 or earlier says the pair of wires is twisted. 'The twist' in the third sentence has no antecedent. The figure's drawn words say only 'copper', and 'twisted pair' appears only in the invisible desc.
judge_fix: Replace 'That is the trick behind the twist.' with: 'That is the trick behind the twisted pair, the two wires of a cable wound around each other.' Leave the later 'The twist keeps neither wire systematically closer...' as is.

quote: Given a channel of bandwidth B hertz and signal-to-noise ratio SNR
problem: Bandwidth is never explained anywhere in the book. The reader's everyday meaning (internet speed in Mbps) clashes with the unit hertz and makes 'bit rate given bandwidth' sound circular. It is relied on again in p12 ('at most 2B independent pulses per second', 'Bandwidth buys pulses per second'), on Fig 8.4's axis and in the caption's '3.4 kHz band'.
fix: bandwidth = the width of the range of frequencies the channel passes, in hertz; the faster the signal can wiggle, the more pulses per second
reason: Verified: bandwidth is not defined anywhere in the book (it appears only in the glossary as 'bandwidth-delay product'). It is the central variable of the central formula. It is reused in p12, Fig 8.4's axis and the caption's '3.4 kHz band', and everyday 'bandwidth = speed' clashes with the unit hertz.
judge_fix: In ch8-shannon-p8: 'Given a channel of bandwidth _B_ hertz (the width of the band of frequencies it passes: the wider the band, the faster the signal can switch) and signal-to-noise ratio _SNR_ ...'

quote: the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N
problem: The reader cannot see why a range of levels is the square root of a power. The derivation's first step therefore has to be taken on trust, in a paragraph whose whole job is to read the formula off the physics.
fix: levels are voltages, and power grows with voltage squared, so a voltage spread is the square root of a power
reason: p12 claims to read the formula 'straight off the physics', but the first step takes the square root of a power with no reason. The reason is one clause: power goes as voltage squared. Without it the derivation looks arbitrary.
judge_fix: In ch8-shannon-p12: '... the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N (power grows as the square of the voltage, so a voltage spread is the square root of a power), so the number of reliably distinguishable levels is their ratio: √(1+SNR).'

quote: A phone line at 30 dB allows about 10 bits per hertz
problem: A reader who puts 30 into B · log₂(1 + SNR) gets about 5, not 10. Nothing says that the formula's SNR is a plain power ratio and that 30 dB means the signal is 1,000 times the noise. ch8-substrates-p2 defined decibels only as cable loss.
fix: (30 dB: the signal is 1,000 times the noise, and log₂ 1,001 ≈ 10)
reason: Verified arithmetic. Plugging 30 into log₂(1+SNR) gives about 5, while 30 dB = ratio 1,000 gives log₂(1001) ≈ 9.97 (about 10). 20 dB = 100 gives log₂(101) ≈ 6.66, matching Wi-Fi 6's 6.7. ch8-substrates-p2 does define decibels, but nothing links dB to the formula's SNR, and Fig 8.4's axis is in dB.
judge_fix: In the caption (ch8-shannon-p11): 'A phone line at 30 dB (the signal 1,000 times the noise) allows about 10 bits per hertz, about 34 kbps over the 3.4 kHz band a V.34 modem uses; ...'. Optionally add 'a plain ratio (30 dB is 1,000)' to SNR in p8.

quote: there exists a coding scheme that achieves arbitrarily low error rate
problem: Error-correcting coding is never explained in the section or earlier. The reader does not know that a code adds redundant bits so the receiver can find and fix flipped ones, so cannot see how any 'coding' beats noise. Worse, p6 just used 'coding' for compression, which removes redundancy, the opposite job.
fix: one clause: an error-correcting code adds extra check bits so the receiver can repair errors, spending some rate to buy reliability
reason: The theorem's whole content is that a code can beat noise, and the book never says how. p6 has just used 'coding' for compression (removing redundancy), the opposite job, and p10 only names 'error-correcting codes' in its last sentence. One clause fixes the ambiguity and the missing idea.
judge_fix: In ch8-shannon-p10: 'If you transmit at rate _R < C_, there exists a coding scheme (extra check bits added so the receiver can find and repair flipped bits) that achieves arbitrarily low error rate.'

quote: H = −Σ pᵢ log₂(pᵢ)
problem: p4 defines entropy as the average number of yes-or-no questions, then gives a formula with a minus sign and log₂ of probabilities. Nothing links the two, so the reader cannot explain why this formula counts questions.
fix: a symbol with chance 1/8 is pinned down by 3 halving questions (log₂ 8 = −log₂ ⅛); entropy averages that over symbols, weighted by how often each comes
reason: p4 defines entropy as a count of questions, then p5 gives −Σ p log₂ p with no bridge. The log is the unexplained step, and the reader cannot see why this formula counts questions. A single worked symbol links them without adding expert detail.
judge_fix: In ch8-shannon-p6, after 'Measured in bits per symbol.': 'Each term is the questions one symbol costs: a symbol with chance ⅛ is pinned down by three halving questions (log₂ 8 = −log₂ ⅛), and entropy averages those costs, weighted by how often each symbol comes.'

quote: a long run of them can be stored in about 0.81 bits per flip
problem: From ch2-binary the reader knows that n bits name only 2^n outcomes, so 100 flips seem to need 100 bits. How grouping flips gets below one bit per flip is never shown.
fix: give the likely runs short codes and the rare ones longer codes, so the average falls below one bit per flip
reason: Under 1 bit per flip contradicts what ch2 taught (n bits name 2^n outcomes). The mechanism is the surprise, and p6 says only 'coding several flips at a time'. One clause supplies it.
judge_fix: In ch8-shannon-p6: 'coding several flips at a time, with short codes for the likely runs and longer ones for the rare runs, a long run of them can be stored in about 0.81 bits per flip.'

quote: the entire stream is corrupted from there onward
problem: The reader cannot see why one miscounted flat stretch spoils every bit after it instead of adding one wrong bit. Fig 8.6 then shows the bits after the run (1 1) read correctly, which looks like a contradiction and sends the reader back to p2.
fix: one clause: an extra or missing bit pushes every later bit one place out, so everything after it is misread
reason: 'The entire stream is corrupted' is overstated against Fig 8.6. The figure shows the bits after the flat stretch (1 1) read correctly, only one place late, so it looks like a contradiction. The accurate mechanism is a slipped count that shifts everything after it.
judge_fix: In ch8-encoding-p2, replace the last sentence with: 'Drift even slightly out of sync and the receiver counts one bit too many or too few, so every bit after it lands one place out.'

quote: every Ethernet frame still carries the header structure invented for that shared cable
problem: Nothing in the section or earlier says what an Ethernet frame is or what its header holds, yet frames carry the rest of the section (Fig 8.9, Fig 8.10, p10, p11). The reader also can't see why a shared cable needed addresses at all. MAC addresses only arrive at p7.
fix: one clause: a frame is one chunk of data on the wire, and its header names the destination and source MAC, so on a shared cable each card keeps only frames addressed to it (MAC explained later at p7)
reason: 'Frame' first appears here in ch8-ethernet-p4, and the only earlier use in the book is 'stack frame'. It is then used in Figs 8.9 and 8.10 and p10. The gloss can be given at first use. MAC addresses are explained at p7 and the sentence already names them, so the header only needs a pointer to what it does.
judge_fix: In ch8-ethernet-p4: 'But every Ethernet frame, the unit of data on the wire, still carries a header built for that shared cable, which names sender and receiver by 48-bit MAC address.'

quote: Each then waits a random number of slots, so one goes first
problem: 'Slot' is never defined, so the reader doesn't know how long one is. They just watched B start because A's signal hadn't reached it yet, so they can't see why waiting one slot means B will now find the line busy instead of colliding again.
fix: define the slot as a fixed wait long enough for a signal to cross the whole cable and back, so a station waiting one slot hears one that went at zero
reason: 'Slot' is never defined anywhere, yet backoff only makes sense with it. B had just collided because A's signal had not reached it. Waiting one slot works because a slot is at least as long as a signal's trip across the cable and back, so B then hears A. Without this the figure's 'B waits 1 slot, line busy' is an unexplained jump. The caption stays at two sentences.
judge_fix: Caption ch8-ethernet-p6: 'Two stations hear a quiet cable and start at almost the same moment; their signals collide, both notice, jam and stop. Each then waits a random number of slots (a slot is the time a signal needs to cross the whole cable and back), so one goes first while the other finds the line busy and waits its turn.'

quote: rapidly send frames with a million different fabricated source MACs
problem: p7 said the MAC is burned into the card at manufacture, so the reader can't see how one machine on one port can send a million different source addresses. Nothing says that the source field of a frame is just bits the sender writes and that nobody checks them.
fix: one clause: the burned-in address is only a default; software writes each frame's source field, and the switch takes it on trust
reason: p7 says the MAC is 'burned into the network card', then the strip has an attacker sending a million 'fabricated source MACs' from one port, which looks contradictory. The missing fact is that the source field is just bits written by software and nobody checks it.
judge_fix: In ch8-ethernet-p11: '... send frames with a million different fabricated source MACs (the burned-in address is only a default: software writes each frame's source field, and the switch takes it on trust).'

quote: fills the table to capacity, and falls back to what it does
problem: The reader learned from Fig 8.10 that the switch already knows where A and B sit, so 'table full' doesn't explain why it would stop knowing where real destinations are and start flooding.
fix: one step: the fake entries crowd out the real ones (or outlast them when they expire and cannot be relearned), so real destinations become unknown and are flooded
reason: The reader has seen the switch learn A and B (Fig 8.10), so 'table full, therefore flood' skips the step that makes the attack work: real entries age out or are pushed out and cannot be relearned, because the table is stuffed with fakes. The fix is one clause and fits the strip's earlier 'entries expire' note.
judge_fix: In ch8-ethernet-p11: 'The switch records each one, fills the table to capacity, and so can no longer keep or relearn the real entries as they expire; with real destinations unknown, it falls back to what it does when it does not know which port a destination MAC sits on: _broadcast to every port_.'

quote: packets that need to find their way across that graph
problem: 'That graph' points at nothing: the book never uses 'graph' for a network of nodes and links, and the only graphs in Chapter 8 are plotted curves (Figs 8.3, 8.4). The antecedent, p2's 'global graph of nodes', was cut in the law-4 rewrite (f01c84e) and replaced with 'many networks joined together', so this reference no longer points at anything.
fix: 'across that web of networks' (or 'across them'), with no graph word
reason: Verified: 'that graph' has no antecedent in ch8. The only 'graph' mentions in Part III are in Ch9 (where it is the book's metaphor for the internet). The cut of p2's earlier wording leaves a dangling pronoun in the seam. The fix is trivial and keeps Ch9's own 'graph' introduction intact.
judge_fix: In ch8-layers-p6: '... and packets that need to find their way across all of them from any source to any destination.'

quote: copper | Ethernet, up to 100 m
problem: This brings back an error the ledger already fixed (UNDER.md §4g, the 'Fig 8.2: the router-to-provider hop' row). The 100 m limit applies to an Ethernet run inside a building. The router-to-provider hop is DSL over telephone pair (a few km), cable coax or fibre. Pass 28 changed the label to 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km' and the desc to 'Ethernet to 100 m, DSL for a few kilometres' (bf00333). The Pass 30 Gate 2 repair (93184ba) put back 'Ethernet, up to 100 m', and the desc now reads 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (twisted pair: Ethernet, up to 100 m per run)'. Ledger law: re-introducing a corrected error is a failed pass.
fix: Label under 'copper': 'DSL or coax, a few km' (or restore 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km'). Desc: 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (a telephone pair carrying DSL for a few kilometres, or cable coax) or on fibre.' The 'Copper' item in the How it works strip can stay as it is: it describes Ethernet runs in general.
reason: Verified in public/part-3.html: the label reads 'Ethernet, up to 100 m' and the desc reads 'twisted pair: Ethernet, up to 100 m per run'. UNDER.md §4g (line 582) corrected exactly this on 2026-10-11 (the 100 m limit is a LAN run; the provider hop is DSL, coax or fibre). Commit 93184ba replaced 'Ethernet 100 m, DSL km' with 'Ethernet, up to 100 m', so the error is back. Ledger law applies.
judge_fix: Label under 'copper' (about 20 characters, fits the slot): 'phone line, a few km'. The 'DSL' abbreviation stays out, since Gate 2 removed it as untaught. Desc: 'From router to internet provider it travels on copper (a telephone line or TV cable, a few kilometres) or on fibre.' Leave the 'Copper' strip item, which is about Ethernet runs in general. Update docs/pass-30-figures.md line 205 if it quotes the old wording.

quote: How do you keep a voltage signal recognisable after a kilometre of copper? After a hundred kilometres of fibre?
problem: Fibre carries no voltage signal. It carries light, as ch8-substrates-p3 and Fig 8.1 say. The paragraph's last sentence, 'The voltage on a wire is the substrate', repeats the copper-only framing for a chapter about copper, fibre and radio. This is the same error class as the corrected Fig 8.1 caption.
fix: 'How do you keep a signal recognisable after a kilometre of copper? After a hundred kilometres of fibre? ...' and 'The signal on the medium is the substrate; everything else in the next five chapters is what we build on top of it.'
reason: Verified in the HTML. ch8-bridge-p3 asks how to keep a 'voltage signal' recognisable 'after a hundred kilometres of fibre' and closes 'The voltage on a wire is the substrate'. Fibre carries light, as p1, ch8-substrates-p3 and Fig 8.1 all say, and the chapter covers copper, fibre and radio. Same error class as the corrected Fig 8.1 caption.
judge_fix: 'How do you keep a signal recognisable after a kilometre of copper? After a hundred kilometres of fibre? Over a wireless link through a forest in the rain? The answers come from physics, mathematics, and practitioner cleverness. The physical signal is the substrate; everything else in the next five chapters is what we build on top of it.'

quote: now in the Computer History Museum, is a hand-drawn diagram on a piece of yellow paper, dated "May 22, 1973" in the corner
problem: No source found supports these specifics. The sketches are hand-drawn diagrams in Metcalfe's typed memo of 22 May 1973, written on an IBM Selectric with the subject 'Ether Acquisition' (CHM, This Day in History, May 22). The well-known reproduction is a composite of those sketches, credited to PARC (digibarn.com/collections/diagrams/ethernet-original). No source found mentions yellow paper, a date in the corner, or the museum holding the original. Also, 'the basic architecture of every wired LAN since' contradicts p4: switched stars replaced the shared cable it draws.
fix: 'His first Ethernet memo, typed on 22 May 1973 and full of hand-drawn diagrams, shows the idea: many computers tapped onto one shared cable, the "ether".' Drop the museum, paper and corner details, and drop 'every wired LAN since' (or say 'every Ethernet frame since', which p4 supports).
reason: Only part of this is sourced. The 22 May 1973 memo ('Ether Acquisition', typed on an IBM Selectric with hand-drawn diagrams) is documented by CHM This Day in History and DigiBarn, whose image is a PARC-credited composite of sketches from the memo. No source found mentions yellow paper, a date written in a corner, or the museum holding the original. 'The basic architecture of every wired LAN since' also over-claims, because p4 itself says switched stars replaced the shared cable.
judge_fix: Replace the two sentences from 'His original Ethernet sketch' on with: 'His first Ethernet memo, dated May 22, 1973 and full of hand-drawn diagrams, shows the architecture: many machines tapped onto one shared cable, the "ether".'

quote: Metcalfe analysed the math on the plane home
problem: The documented sequence is different. Metcalfe read Abramson's 1970 ALOHA paper in spring 1972, and the thesis was rejected in June 1972. He then spent months in Hawaii modelling ALOHAnet with Abramson's students and presented the results at a University of Hawaii conference. He returned to PARC in late October 1972 and added the analysis to the thesis in May 1973 (historyofcomputercommunications.info, section 8.7). His main finding was that a realistic, finite-user ALOHA becomes unstable under heavy load unless stations back off. 'On the plane home' is an embellishment.
fix: 'He spent the next months there modelling ALOHAnet, found that under heavy load its retransmissions could swamp the channel unless stations backed off and waited, wrote that analysis into a revised thesis, and got his doctorate in 1973.'
reason: 'Analysed the math on the plane home' is an embellishment. Sources (historyofcomputercommunications.info 8.7, UH/ACM accounts) say Metcalfe read Abramson's ALOHA paper before the trip, worked in Hawaii for weeks building models, and found ALOHA became unstable under heavy load. He added the analysis to the revised thesis, accepted in 1973. Low severity, but it is a vivid invented detail in a book with a fact ledger.
judge_fix: 'Metcalfe spent weeks there modelling the system, realised Abramson had badly underestimated how much of the channel's time could carry data with smarter timing, wrote the corrections into a revised thesis, and got his doctorate.' (Only 'analysed the math on the plane home' becomes 'spent weeks there modelling the system'.)

quote: WPA2 (2004, broken 2017 by the KRACK attack) to WPA3 (2018, still standing)
problem: The sentence calls WPA2 'broken' by KRACK, a flaw fixed by patches. By the same measure WPA3 did not stay unbroken: the 2019 Dragonblood attacks (Vanhoef and Ronen) recovered passwords from WPA3-SAE through timing and cache side channels and a transition-mode downgrade. Patches and a spec update followed (papers.mathyvanhoef.com/dragonblood.pdf).
fix: '... to WPA3 (2018; the flaws found in it in 2019 were patched, and it still stands)', or simply 'WPA3 (2018)'.
reason: By the paragraph's own measure (WPA 'broken 2008', WPA2 'broken 2017 by KRACK', both patched), WPA3 was also broken: Dragonblood (Vanhoef and Ronen, 2019) attacked its SAE handshake, and it was patched. 'Still standing' is a flat claim a checking owner can falsify. Low severity.
judge_fix: '... to *WPA3* (2018; the flaws found in it in 2019 were patched), is the engineering response to the fact that on a radio link, the attacker is always already in the room.'

quote: Raspberry Pi devices begin `B8:27:EB`
problem: Only boards up to the Pi 3 use B8:27:EB. The Pi 4 and 400 use the Raspberry Pi Ltd prefixes DC:A6:32 or E4:5F:01 (Raspberry Pi whitepaper RP-003474, 'Changing MAC addresses'), and the Pi 5 uses others again. A reader who checks a current Pi will see a different prefix.
fix: 'older Raspberry Pi boards begin `B8:27:EB`, newer ones `DC:A6:32` and others; Apple's begin `00:03:93` or any of a few hundred other prefixes.' (Fig 8.9's 'B8:27:EB = Raspberry Pi Foundation' is correct and can stay.)
reason: B8:27:EB covers boards up to the Pi 3 and Zero W. The Pi 4, 400 and 5 use other Raspberry Pi Ltd prefixes (DC:A6:32, E4:5F:01 and others). A reader who checks a current Pi sees a different prefix. Fig 8.9 and its caption ('B8:27:EB is the Raspberry Pi Foundation') are correct and stay.
judge_fix: '... Older Raspberry Pi boards begin `B8:27:EB`, newer ones `DC:A6:32` and other prefixes; Apple's begin `00:03:93` or any of a few hundred other prefixes.'

quote: both directions on separate wire pairs (full duplex)
problem: True of 10BASE-T and 100BASE-TX only. Gigabit Ethernet (1000BASE-T), the usual link today, sends both directions on all four pairs at once and separates them by echo cancellation. Full duplex does not need separate pairs.
fix: 'With one device per switch port and both ends able to send at the same time (full duplex), collision detection never fires.'
reason: Fig 8.10's strip says full duplex means 'both directions on separate wire pairs'. That is true of 10/100BASE-T only. Gigabit copper (1000BASE-T), the common link today, sends both directions on all four pairs at once using echo cancellation. The fix is shorter and correct.
judge_fix: '*No more collisions.* With one device per switch port and both ends able to send at the same time (full duplex), collision detection never fires.'

quote: cellular at 700 MHz to several GHz
problem: Contradicts the figure's own strip ('from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz') and the §4g Fig 8.2 correction ('cellular uses bands below 1 GHz as well as up to tens of GHz'). 5G millimetre-wave bands sit at 24 to 47 GHz, and 600 MHz bands (e.g. band 71) are in use.
fix: 'cellular from about 600 MHz to tens of GHz'
reason: ch8-substrates-p4 says cellular runs '700 MHz to several GHz' and Wi-Fi '2.4 GHz and 5 GHz'. The Fig 8.2 strip says cellular 'from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz' and Wi-Fi '2.4, 5 and 6 GHz', and §4g (line 553) fixed the figure for this reason (5G mmWave is 24 to 47 GHz; 600 MHz bands exist). The prose and its own figure now disagree. The duplicate findings 16 (same cellular and Wi-Fi point) and 15 are folded in here and at n1.
judge_fix: 'Wi-Fi runs around 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.'

quote: TEMPEST, a US classification programme dating to the 1960s
problem: TEMPEST is not a classification programme. It is the NSA codename for an emission-security specification, with a NATO certification alongside. The shielding standards date from the late 1950s: NAG-1 in 1958, then Directive 5200.19 in 1964 and NSA implementation in 1966 (Wikipedia, 'Tempest (codename)').
fix: 'This is the basis of *TEMPEST*, the NSA codename for standards, set from the late 1950s, for shielding sensitive equipment against precisely this.'
reason: TEMPEST is the NSA codename for emission-security standards (NAG-1 in 1958, Directive 5200.19 in 1964), not a 'classification programme'. 'Dating to the 1960s' is acceptable for the codename and directive. Finding 18 is the same point and is folded in here.
judge_fix: 'This is the basis of *TEMPEST*, the US codename for standards, dating to the 1960s, for shielding sensitive equipment against precisely this.'

problem: p5: 'an unshielded monitor could be reconstructed'. What Van Eck reconstructed was the picture on the monitor, not the monitor. A wording slip.
reason: Van Eck reconstructed the picture displayed on the monitor, not the monitor. 'An unshielded monitor could be reconstructed' is a real wording slip a careful reader trips on. It sits in the same sentence run as n11.
judge_fix: '(Van Eck showed in 1985 that the picture on an unshielded monitor could be reconstructed from across the street; a modern software radio does the same to a leaky cable from across a room.)'

problem: ch8-shannon-p1: 'Before this paper, "amount of information" was a metaphor' overstates it. Hartley (1928, 'Transmission of Information', Bell System Technical Journal) had already defined a quantitative measure of information, the log of the number of possible messages, and Nyquist (1924) worked along the same line. The callout's own title, Shannon–Hartley, names him.
reason: 'Before this paper, "amount of information" was a metaphor' overstates it. Hartley (1928) had defined a quantitative measure (log of the number of possible messages), and the callout two paragraphs later is titled 'Shannon–Hartley' without ever saying who Hartley was. A reader who knows Hartley will stop here. Low severity, and the fix also pays off the callout title.
judge_fix: 'Before this paper, "amount of information" was close to a metaphor (Hartley had only counted equally likely messages, in 1928). After it, information had units (bits) and a formula (entropy).'

problem: ch8-layers-p2: 'Data Link moves frames between machines joined directly by one cable or radio link' says less than the previous section just taught. In switched Ethernet (ch8-ethernet-p4, Fig 8.10) each host has its own cable to the switch, and frames cross the switch between two cables. Wi-Fi frames likewise pass through the access point. The link layer reaches the whole local network, not one cable. A reader fresh from Fig 8.10 may notice the clash. Suggested wording: 'between machines on the same local network'.
reason: ch8-layers-p2 says Data Link moves frames 'between machines joined directly by one cable or radio link'. The section just before it (ch8-ethernet-p4, Fig 8.10) teaches that in switched Ethernet each host has its own cable to a switch and frames cross the switch to reach another host. A reader fresh from Fig 8.10 sees the clash. The same holds for Wi-Fi frames passing through the access point.
judge_fix: 'Data Link moves frames between machines on the same local network, over cable, switch or radio link.'

problem: Three rhetorical questions stand in for explanation, and the answer is a reflexive triplet that teaches nothing ('physics, mathematics, and practitioner cleverness'). The closing clause restates p1. 'The next five chapters' is ambiguous: read from inside Chapter 8, it seems to mean Ch9 to Ch13.

quote: That is the trick behind the twist.
problem: 'The twist' is used as if the reader already knew about it. The paragraph never says that the two wires are twisted around each other (a twisted pair). It also credits the twist with the trick, which is really the difference signal; the twist only supports it, as the paragraph's next-but-one sentence says.
fix: 'The signal is the voltage difference between two wires twisted around each other (a twisted pair), and the receiver reads only that difference.' Then delete 'That is the trick behind the twist.' and keep 'The twist keeps neither wire systematically closer...'.
reason: ch8-substrates-p2 never says the wires are twisted. 'the trick behind the twist' and 'The twist keeps ...' refer to something the reader has not met; 'twisted pair' appears only in the invisible <desc>. The trick sentence also credits the twist with what the difference signal does.
judge_fix: '*Copper* is the original. The signal is the voltage _difference_ between two wires twisted around each other (a twisted pair), and the receiver reads only that difference.' Delete 'That is the trick behind the twist.' Keep the next sentence and 'The twist keeps neither wire systematically closer to any noise source, so the two stay balanced along the whole run.'

quote: Wi-Fi runs around 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz; cellular at 700 MHz to several GHz
problem: These numbers disagree with Fig 8.2. Its <desc> and strip give Wi-Fi as 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz and cellular as 'below 1 GHz to tens of GHz', the range §4g row 553 settled.
fix: 'Wi-Fi runs at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.'
reason: ch8-substrates-p4 says Wi-Fi at '2.4 GHz and 5 GHz' and cellular '700 MHz to several GHz'. Fig 8.2 (desc and strip) says Wi-Fi 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz and cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz, the range settled in the §4g row for Fig 8.2. Prose and figure disagree on the same facts.
judge_fix: 'Wi-Fi runs at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.'

quote: allowing tens to hundreds of kilometres between repeaters
problem: Three different spacings appear in the chapter. p3 says 'tens to hundreds of kilometres', the Fig 8.1 caption says 'repeaters every 50 to 100 km', and the Fig 8.2 strip says 'tens of kilometres between amplifiers'.
fix: Pick one figure and use it everywhere, e.g. p3: 'allowing 50 to 100 km between repeaters on an undersea cable', matching Fig 8.1. Drop the spacing from the Fig 8.2 strip.
reason: Typical amplifier spacing is about 50 to 100 km: 0.2 dB/km gives 10 to 20 dB per span, and the Fig 8.1 caption says 50 to 100 km. 'tens to hundreds of kilometres between repeaters' in p3 overstates it, since hundreds of km applies only to special unrepeatered links.
judge_fix: p3: '... about 0.2 dB per kilometre, so repeaters can sit tens of kilometres apart (50 to 100 km on an undersea cable).' The Fig 8.2 strip 'tens of kilometres between amplifiers' is then already consistent; leave it.

quote: an unshielded monitor could be reconstructed from across the street
problem: Wrong words: what Van Eck reconstructed was the picture on the monitor, not the monitor. The earlier sentence also ends in a circular 'This is the basis of TEMPEST ... against precisely this'.
fix: '(Van Eck showed in 1985 that the picture on an unshielded monitor could be rebuilt from its emissions across the street; ...)'. Earlier: 'TEMPEST, a US programme dating to the 1960s, sets the shielding standards that guard against it.'
reason: What Van Eck reconstructed was the picture shown on a CRT monitor, not the monitor. 'an unshielded monitor could be reconstructed' is a wrong word. Source: W. van Eck, 'Electromagnetic Radiation from Video Display Units: An Eavesdropping Risk?', Computers & Security, 1985. The TEMPEST sentence is acceptable and should be left alone.
judge_fix: '(Van Eck showed in 1985 that the picture on an unshielded monitor could be rebuilt from its emissions across the street; a modern software radio does the same to a leaky cable from across a room.)'

quote: A source that always sends the same symbol carries no information; a fair coin carries one full bit per flip
problem: The caption restates p6: a fair coin gives 1 bit, a constant source gives 0, and entropy is the compression floor. It also brings a second biased example (90/10 gives 0.47) while the prose uses another (3/4, 1/4 gives 0.81). That is two examples where one works, and the prose's example is not in the picture.
fix: Caption: 'Entropy of a two-symbol source against p, the chance of a 1; a 90/10 source is marked at 0.47 bits.' In p6, use the figure's example: 'A coin that lands heads nine times in ten gives H ≈ 0.47 bits: coded several flips at a time, a long run of them fits in about 0.47 bits per flip.'
reason: The prose uses a 3/4-1/4 coin (0.81 bits), while the figure and caption use a 90/10 source (0.47 bits). Two biased examples where one works, and the prose one is not drawn. The caption's first sentence also restates p6.
judge_fix: p6: 'A coin that lands heads nine times in ten (0.9, 0.1) gives H ≈ 0.47 bits: if you code several flips at a time, a long run of them fits in about 0.47 bits per flip.' Caption: 'Entropy of a two-symbol source against p, the chance of a 1: 0 when every symbol is predictable, 1 bit for the fair coin, symmetric between. A 90/10 source is marked at 0.47 bits, the least any lossless code can average for it.'

quote: coding several flips at a time, a long run of them can be stored in about 0.81 bits per flip
problem: Dangling modifier: grammatically the 'long run' is what does the coding, so the reader has to reread the sentence.
fix: '...: if you code several flips at a time, a long run of them fits in about 0.81 bits per flip.' (0.47 if the 90/10 example is adopted.)
reason: Dangling modifier in p6: 'coding several flips at a time, a long run of them can be stored ...' makes the run do the coding. It is a small fix and it is folded into the finding 17 rewrite.
judge_fix: 'if you code several flips at a time, a long run of them fits in about 0.47 bits per flip' (use the 0.81 figure if the 3/4 example is kept).

quote: sits somewhere on Shannon's curve, fighting for the last bit.
problem: An aphorism closes the callout. 'Shannon's curve' points to a figure the reader has not yet reached, and that figure plots a two-symbol source, which no compressor sits on.
fix: 'Every lossless compressor, ZIP and PNG included, is judged by how close it comes to that floor.'
reason: 'sits somewhere on Shannon's curve' is inaccurate: the curve is the floor, and real compressors sit at or above it, not on it. The curve plots a two-symbol source, which no compressor sits on. The closing aphorism adds nothing.
judge_fix: 'Every lossless compressor, ZIP and PNG included, is judged by how close it gets to that floor.'

quote: Given a channel of bandwidth B hertz and signal-to-noise ratio SNR
problem: 'Bandwidth' measured in hertz is never defined. The baseline reader knows 'bandwidth' as a data rate (Mbps), which here is exactly the wrong meaning. The formula and Fig 8.4 depend on it, and Section 04 then says 'double bandwidth'.
fix: 'Given a channel of bandwidth B hertz (the width of the range of frequencies it passes, not its bit rate) and signal-to-noise ratio SNR (signal power divided by noise power), ...'
reason: 'bandwidth B hertz' is used in the central formula, in Fig 8.4 and in Section 04. It is never defined, and a baseline reader's meaning (Mbps) is exactly wrong here. p12 only hints at it through 2B pulses.
judge_fix: 'Given a channel of bandwidth _B_ hertz (the width of the range of frequencies it passes, not its bit rate) and signal-to-noise ratio _SNR_ (signal power divided by noise power), the maximum reliable bit rate, the **channel capacity**, is:'

quote: the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N
problem: A step is skipped. Nothing says why powers turn into square roots: a signal's voltage grows as the square root of its power. A reader with school maths stops here, and the rest of the derivation depends on it.
fix: '...with signal power S and noise power N (a voltage grows as the square root of the power it carries), the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N, ...'
reason: p12 goes from powers S and N to √(S+N) and √N with no reason given. The unstated step is that a signal's voltage grows as the square root of the power. The whole derivation depends on it.
judge_fix: '... with signal power S and noise power N (a voltage grows as the square root of the power it carries), the received range spans about √(S+N) and the blur is about √N, ...'

quote: there exists a coding scheme that achieves arbitrarily low error rate
problem: The theorem rests on 'coding scheme', which is never explained. The reader cannot say how a code beats noise (by adding redundancy). Section 04 then uses 'encoding' for line codes, a different thing, which invites confusion. As written it is a slogan in place of the mechanism (law 4).
fix: '...there exists a coding scheme (a way of adding redundant bits so the receiver can find and repair what the noise damaged) that achieves arbitrarily low error rate.'
reason: 'coding scheme' is the heart of the theorem but is never explained. 'no matter how clever the encoding' also collides with Section 04, where 'encoding' means line codes.
judge_fix: '... there exists a coding scheme (a way of adding redundant bits so the receiver can find and repair what the noise damaged) that achieves arbitrarily low error rate. If R > C, errors are inevitable, no matter how clever the coding.'

quote: Shannon–Hartley channel capacity
problem: The callout label names Hartley, who appears nowhere in the chapter. p12 credits only Nyquist, and p1 says that before 1948 'amount of information' was only a metaphor, so the reader is left asking who Hartley was.
fix: In p8: '...the channel capacity, named for Shannon and Ralph Hartley, a Bell Labs engineer who first counted distinguishable signal levels in 1928, is:' (source Hartley 1928, 'Transmission of Information', BSTJ, before adding it).
reason: The callout label 'Shannon–Hartley' names Hartley, who appears nowhere in the chapter. The label stays a puzzle, and the body credits only Nyquist.
judge_fix: Shortest repair: relabel the callout 'Channel capacity'. The alternative is a clause in p8: 'the **channel capacity** (the Shannon–Hartley theorem, after Ralph Hartley, who counted distinguishable signal levels at Bell Labs in 1928)'. Check Hartley, 'Transmission of Information', BSTJ 7(3), 1928, before adding it.

quote: The signal sits at one of two levels and only changes when a new bit arrives.
problem: Wrong: NRZ changes only when the next bit differs from the last one. As written it says the line changes on every bit, which contradicts the next sentence's flat line for a run of equal bits.
fix: 'The signal sits at one of two levels and changes only when a bit differs from the one before it.'
reason: 'only changes when a new bit arrives' can be read as 'changes on every new bit', which the very next sentence (a long run looks like a flat line) contradicts. Rewording is cheap and exact.
judge_fix: 'The signal sits at one of two levels and changes only when a bit differs from the one before it.'

quote: Manchester code puts a transition in the middle of every bit: rising for a 1, falling for a 0.
problem: The caption restates p3: mid-bit transition, rising for 1, clock recovered, the cost. The cost alone appears four times (p3 'double bandwidth', this caption, the Fig 8.5 strip '20 million signal changes', the Fig 8.6 caption 'up to twice the signal changes').

The cost appears again in the strip and in the Fig 8.6 caption. Law 2 and law 3 ask the caption to name the picture and leave the explanation to the prose.
judge_fix: Fig 8.5 caption: 'The bits 1 0 1 1 0 0 1 in Manchester code: each mid-bit edge gives the bit and keeps the receiver's clock in step.' Fig 8.6 caption: drop ', at the cost of up to twice the signal changes'.

quote: so it corrects its clock each time and reads all seven
problem: 'All seven' right after 'four zeros ... reads five' can be read as seven zeros. The reader has to work out that it means the seven bits.
fix: '...so it corrects its clock each time and reads all seven bits correctly.'

judge_fix: '... so the receiver reads five zeros. Manchester gives it an edge in every bit, so it corrects its clock each time and reads all seven bits correctly, at the cost of up to twice the signal changes.'

quote: A carrier wave has three things a transmitter can change: its size (AM), how fast it oscillates (FM)
problem: The caption repeats p6 almost word for word: size/AM, how fast it oscillates/FM, phase/PSK, QAM changing size and phase together. The strip's 'The carrier' bullet repeats p6's 'a frequency the medium carries well' as well.
fix: Caption: 'The bits 1 0 1 0 carried three ways: the wave's size, its speed or its starting direction changes with each bit.' Cut the strip's 'The carrier' bullet.
reason: The Fig 8.7 caption's first sentence is ch8-encoding-p6 nearly verbatim (size/AM, how fast it oscillates/FM, phase/PSK, QAM). The strip's 'The carrier' bullet repeats p6's 'a frequency the medium carries well'. A caption should name the picture.
judge_fix: Caption: 'The bits 1 0 1 0 carried three ways: with each bit the wave's size, its speed or its starting direction changes. Wi-Fi and cable modems change size and phase together (QAM), packing many bits into each symbol: up to 10 in Wi-Fi 6, but only on a far cleaner signal than the 20 dB point in Fig 8.4.' Cut the strip's 'The carrier' bullet.

quote: packing many bits into each symbol: 10 in Wi-Fi 6.
problem: Fig 8.4 says Wi-Fi 6 at about 20 dB is allowed 6.7 bits per hertz. Here Wi-Fi 6 packs 10 bits per symbol, and nothing reconciles the two numbers. A careful reader will think the book has Wi-Fi beating Shannon's limit.
fix: '...packing many bits into each symbol: up to 10 in Wi-Fi 6, on a strong clean signal well above the 20 dB that holds it to 6.7 in Fig 8.4.'
reason: A careful reader sets Fig 8.4's 'Wi-Fi 6 at about 20 dB allows 6.7 bits per hertz' against '10 bits' per symbol in Wi-Fi 6 and suspects a Shannon violation. Bits per symbol and bits per hertz differ, and 10 bits per symbol needs a far cleaner signal (the Shannon bound for 10 b/Hz is about 30 dB). Nothing reconciles the two numbers.
judge_fix: Use the caption wording in the fix for finding 31: 'packing many bits into each symbol: up to 10 in Wi-Fi 6, but only on a far cleaner signal than the 20 dB point in Fig 8.4.'

quote: Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024, 10 bits, and Wi-Fi 7 4096, 12 bits, when the signal is clean
problem: Too many commas: the numbers and bit counts run together, and the sentence has to be read twice.
fix: 'Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024 combinations (10 bits) and Wi-Fi 7 uses 4096 (12 bits) when the signal is clean, dropping to fewer as it degrades.'

judge_fix: '16 combinations of size and phase carry 4 bits per symbol; Wi-Fi 6 uses 1024 combinations (10 bits) and Wi-Fi 7 uses 4096 (12 bits) when the signal is clean, dropping to fewer as it degrades.'

quote: In ever faster versions of itself, it became the dominant local-area networking technology on the planet.
problem: Grammatically 'it' is the CSMA/CD rule named just before. Read that way, the sentence contradicts p4, which says switches ended collisions and the collision machinery now sits unused.
fix: 'In ever faster versions, Ethernet became the dominant local-area networking technology on the planet.'
reason: In ch8-ethernet-p1 the antecedent of 'it' is the CSMA/CD rule named just before. Read that way, it contradicts p4 (collision machinery now sits unused).
judge_fix: 'In ever faster versions, Ethernet became the dominant local-area networking technology on the planet.'

quote: But every Ethernet frame still carries the header structure invented for that shared cable, including the 48-bit MAC addresses.
problem: 'Frame' and 'header' are never explained in this chapter or earlier, and MAC addresses only arrive three paragraphs later (p7). Frames are then relied on in Figs 8.9 and 8.10, p11 and ch8-layers-p2.
fix: 'But every Ethernet frame (the block of bits a station sends in one go) still starts with the header designed for that shared cable: a few fields in front of the data, led by the address of the card it is for and the card it came from, the MAC addresses described below.'
reason: 'frame' and 'header' appear in ch8-ethernet-p4 undefined, and MAC addresses are only explained in p7. Frame is relied on in Figs 8.9 and 8.10, p11 and layers-p2.
judge_fix: 'But every Ethernet frame (the block of bits sent in one go) still starts with a header designed for that shared cable, which includes the 48-bit MAC addresses described below.'

quote: their signals collide, both notice, jam and stop. Each then waits a random number of slots
problem: 'Jam' and 'slots' are explained nowhere in the prose or the caption. Only the closed strip says 'slot times', and only the invisible <desc> says 'jam signal'.
fix: '...their signals collide; both notice, send a short jamming signal so every station knows, and stop. Each then waits a random number of slot times (a fixed short interval), so one goes first...'
reason: The Fig 8.8 caption uses 'jam' as a verb and 'slots' without explanation. The fig words say 'send a jam' and 'wait 0 slots'. A newcomer cannot know what a slot is.
judge_fix: 'Two stations hear a quiet cable and start at almost the same moment; their signals collide, both notice, send a short jamming signal and stop. Each then waits a random number of slots (a fixed short pause), so one goes first while the other finds the line busy and waits its turn.'

quote: Every Ethernet device has a MAC address, a 48-bit identifier burned into the network card
problem: MAC is never spelled out in the chapter. Two sentences later 'Apple's begin 00:03:93', which invites the reader to read MAC as Apple's Mac.
fix: 'Every Ethernet device has a MAC (Media Access Control) address, nothing to do with Apple's Mac: a 48-bit identifier burned into the network card at manufacture.'
reason: 'MAC' is never spelled out, and the next sentence mentions Apple's prefixes, so a reader may take it as Apple's Mac. Facts: B8:27:EB is the Raspberry Pi Foundation's OUI and 00:03:93 is Apple's.
judge_fix: 'Every Ethernet device has a **MAC address** (Media Access Control; no relation to Apple's Mac), a 48-bit identifier burned into the network card at manufacture.'

quote: A MAC address is 48 bits: the first half names the maker (B8:27:EB is the Raspberry Pi Foundation), the second the card.
problem: The caption restates p7 (the two halves, the Raspberry Pi prefix) and p8 (broadcast 'who has 192.168.1.5?', reply, cache). The strip's 'The halves' bullet makes it a third time.
fix: Caption: 'One MAC address split into maker and card, and the ARP exchange that finds it: broadcast, reply, cache.' Cut the strip's 'The halves' bullet.
reason: The Fig 8.9 caption restates p7 (halves, Raspberry Pi prefix) and p8 (broadcast, reply, cache) entirely, and the strip's 'The halves' bullet repeats p7 again.
judge_fix: Caption: 'One MAC address split into maker and card, and the ARP exchange that finds it: broadcast the question, the owner replies, the answer is cached.' Cut the strip's 'The halves' bullet.

quote: the asker caches the answer for a few minutes
problem: The Fig 8.9 strip says entries 'age out after seconds to minutes, depending on the system'. The two numbers disagree.
fix: 'the asker caches the answer for a while (seconds to minutes, depending on the system)', and cut the strip's 'Expiry' bullet.
reason: p8 says 'a few minutes' while the Fig 8.9 strip says 'seconds to minutes, depending on the system'. ARP timeouts do vary: Linux and Windows are tens of seconds, macOS about 20 minutes. The strip is the more accurate of the two.
judge_fix: p8: 'the asker caches the answer for a while (seconds to minutes, depending on the system)'. Keep the strip's Expiry bullet.

quote: falls back to what it does when it does not know which port a destination MAC sits on: broadcast to every port
problem: Fig 8.10 calls this 'flood' and its table 'SWITCH TABLE'. Here it is 'broadcast' and 'MAC table'. The Fig 8.10 strip uses 'broadcast' for something else, frames addressed to everyone. So the reader sees two words for one mechanism and one word for two.
fix: 'A switch's table (Fig 8.10) has finite size...' and '...: flood the frame out of every port.'
reason: ch8-ethernet-p11 uses 'broadcast to every port' for what Fig 8.10 and its caption call 'flood'. The Fig 8.10 strip then uses 'broadcast' for something else (frames addressed to everyone). One mechanism has two names, and one name serves two mechanisms.
judge_fix: '... and falls back to what it does when it does not know which port a destination MAC sits on: _flood the frame out of every port_.' Keep 'MAC table'.

quote: Each layer is a customer of the layer below and a provider for the layer above.
problem: The customer/provider analogy is never cashed out in prose. Encapsulation, the literal mechanism (each layer wraps its data in a header on the way down and removes it on the way up), appears only in the Fig 8.11 caption and strip. The section's central idea therefore lives outside the prose.
fix: Replace the sentence with: 'On the way out, each layer hands its data to the layer below, which wraps it in a header of its own; on arrival each layer removes its header and hands the rest up.' The Fig 8.11 caption can then just name the picture.
reason: The section's central idea, encapsulation (each layer wraps data in its own header going down and removes it going up), appears only in the Fig 8.11 caption and strip. The prose offers only the customer/provider analogy and never cashes it out.
judge_fix: After 'Each layer is a customer of the layer below and a provider for the layer above.' add: 'On the way out, each layer hands its data to the layer below, which wraps it in a header of its own; on arrival each layer removes its header and hands the rest up (Fig 8.11).'

quote: TCP/IP folds OSI's top three layers into one Application layer, because protocols such as HTTP manage their own sessions
problem: p3 already gives the collapse and both of its reasons. The Fig 8.11 caption repeats it ('the top three blur into the application, which is why...'), this caption repeats it with both reasons, and the Fig 8.12 strip ('HTTP as an example') makes it four times.
fix: Fig 8.12 caption: 'The seven OSI layers beside the four TCP/IP layers that run the internet, with the protocols that live in each.' In the Fig 8.11 caption, cut 'In practice the top three blur ... four layers of TCP/IP.'
reason: The collapse of the top three layers into one Application layer is given in p3 with both reasons, repeated in the Fig 8.11 caption, again with both reasons in the Fig 8.12 caption (p5), and a fourth time in the Fig 8.12 strip.
judge_fix: Fig 8.11 caption: cut 'In practice the top three blur into the application, which is why the internet runs on the four layers of TCP/IP.' Fig 8.12 caption: 'The seven OSI layers beside the four TCP/IP layers that run the internet, with the protocols that live in each. OSI says where a feature belongs; TCP/IP describes what is on the wire.'

quote: TLS around the request
problem: TLS and 'GET /' carry the figure's first wrapping, but neither is glossed in any visible text. Only the closed Fig 8.12 strip says TLS encrypts. Both are taught in Chapter 11.
fix: '...: TLS (the encryption Chapter 11 explains) around the request for a page (GET /), then a TCP header, ...'

quote: Bottom to top: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
problem: The prose writes 'Data Link' but Figs 8.11 and 8.12 and the strip write 'Data link'. OSI is never spelled out. p3 calls TCP/IP's middle layer 'the IP layer' but Fig 8.12 calls it 'Internet'.
fix: Use one capitalisation ('Data Link'). Expand on first use: 'the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) seven-layer model'. In p3 write 'the Internet layer, where IP lives'.

judge_fix: p2: 'The canonical reference is the *OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) seven-layer model*, ...'. Use 'Data link' (as in the figures) in p2 and the strip, or 'Data Link' in the figures, so there is one spelling.

quote: on tens of thousands of independently-administered networks, none of them aware of most of the others, and packets that need
problem: An -ly adverb takes no hyphen. The sentence also lists the internet as devices '... and packets that need to find their way', which forces a reread. 'That graph' refers to a graph the chapter never set up.
fix: 'The internet is billions of devices on tens of thousands of independently administered networks, none aware of most of the others, and a packet must find its way across all of them from any source to any destination.'

quote: then B sends
problem: The animation shows B transmitting while A's signal is still on the cable. A's second frame fills the cable from 0.40 to 0.674 of the cycle, but B's bar starts at 0.558. Frame t6.867 shows orange running from A to a third of the way along and blue from there to B. That is the same picture as the opening collision, minus the red block, shown under the label 'then B sends'. It contradicts the desc ('then sends once A has finished') and the carrier-sense rule the figure teaches.

B's second bar starts growing at 0.5583 and the label 'then B sends' appears at 0.5583. So from 0.558 to 0.674 both bars overlap on the wire with B under the label 'then B sends'. Width: values '0;0;268;0;0;0;0' with keyTimes '0;0.247573;0.402913;0.558252;0.810631;0.810680;1'. Add an x animation with the same keyTimes and values '66;66;66;334;334;334;334'. B's bar and the 'then B sends' label stay as they are.

quote: line busy: B waits
problem: The label appears at 0.2765 of the cycle, but A's resent signal reaches B only at 0.4029. In frame t3.433, A's bar is less than halfway along the cable while B already says it hears a busy line. The figure's whole point is that a station hears another only after the signal arrives ('B has not heard it yet').

quote: and the curve is symmetric between them
problem: The curve is symmetric about p = 0.5, which is the fair coin. It is not symmetric 'between' a constant source and a fair coin. The phrasing blurs the symmetry the How it works strip states precisely.
fix: "...a fair coin carries one full bit per flip, and the curve is symmetric about it."
reason: Fig 8.3 caption says the curve 'is symmetric between them' (a constant source and a fair coin). The curve is symmetric about p = 0.5, the fair coin, as the How it works strip says; 'between' is imprecise in a chapter about a mathematical result.
judge_fix: 'A source that always sends the same symbol carries no information; a fair coin carries one full bit per flip, and the curve is symmetric about the fair coin.'
